04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Fiona's message appeared to offer the bridge Emma had been looking for between the trust's decision-notice template and its actual correspondence. The records team had located a ledger labelled “Outgoing letters — Student Travel 2011”, apparently used by the scheme administrator. Its existence was significant; its evidential reach remained narrow.

Fiona described a mixture of reference numbers, dates and empty fields. There had been no reconciliation with completed notices or any postal documentation, and the inventory was still preliminary. Identifiable student details could not be released. Emma requested images of the ledger's structure rather than its entries, explaining that she wanted to understand what the document was designed to record.

The cover and one blank page arrived later that morning. Four headings appeared above the ruled columns: Reference number, Date prepared, Date sent and Notes. The distinction between preparation and dispatch was explicit. There was no corresponding field for acknowledgement of receipt.

“Surely that's evidence they informed the applicants,” Sarah said.

“It's evidence that they designed a register for outgoing notices. Fiona says some lines are marked as sent, but we can't leap from that notation to proof of delivery.”

Sarah pressed the point: administrative records were evidence, weren't they? Emma agreed. The question was evidence of what. An entry could support a limited claim about recorded dispatch, subject to the reliability of the record itself. It could not independently establish that the postal service delivered an envelope, that it contained the correct notice or that a student understood the review deadline.

A separate update from the newspaper archive reinforced the same discipline. Staff had not searched the unpublished correspondence from 2011, and access might be constrained by privacy obligations. Emma logged the enquiry as pending, not as evidence of additional dissatisfied families.

Later Fiona confirmed that a preliminary examination had found some ledger rows bearing dates in the sent column. The team had discovered no corresponding postal receipts so far. Fiona could not say whether every decision had been entered, whether recorded dispatch always occurred or whether surviving pages represented the complete series. She had no basis for linking the anonymous parent's complaint to any particular entry.

Emma was tempted to frame the distinction as a failure of the trust's communication process. But uncertainty cut both ways. The absence of surviving receipts did not prove that letters had failed to arrive. Equally, a neat dispatch column could not demonstrate that the intended recipients had been informed. She opened three categories in her notes—Prepared, Dispatched, Received—and listed the supporting documents she would require for each.

The printed appeal guidance made the issue consequential. Students were supposed to request reconsideration within fourteen days of receiving a decision. The start of that period depended on an event the present records did not establish for any individual: receipt of the notice. Yet Emma still had no evidence that the deadline had been applied unfairly, or even that anyone had attempted a formal appeal.

Sarah suggested pursuing the identity of the administrator. Emma preferred a less intrusive first step. A policy on unsuccessful delivery or unacknowledged correspondence might reveal whether the organisation had anticipated the problem. She asked Fiona whether the procedural files contained instructions for checking that notices reached applicants, and how undelivered letters were handled.

The enquiry did not promise a dramatic revelation. It did something more useful: it identified the exact missing link between an institution's stated procedure and a person's ability to exercise a right.

At the end of her notes Emma wrote one sentence, underlining its final word: A recorded dispatch is not a confirmed receipt.
